name: McGill Big 3

lead: The Big 3 are a curl-up, side bridge and bird dog associated with spine researcher Stuart McGill, used to build trunk endurance with low spinal load. Posture communities fold it into pelvic tilt and back routines for better carriage.

The exercises are described as training abdominal and back muscles to stabilise the spine without bending it repeatedly. McGill is a Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo; no study found tests the Big 3 for appearance.

paras: People do the three exercises as a short routine, often as a warm-up or on rest days, and combine them with stretching and glute work in posture programs.
Low risk in general; back pain is usually referred to a clinician.

angle.text: This three-exercise core routine from spine biomechanist Stuart McGill builds back-sparing trunk strength, and posture circles use it for a steadier trunk and better carriage. Its use for looks has not been studied.

lead: The McGill Big 3 is a trio of core exercises, usually described as a modified curl-up, the side bridge and the bird dog, associated with spine biomechanist Stuart McGill. McGill is a Canadian academic and Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo, a member of the Order of Canada since 2019 and the author of books including Low Back Disorders and Back Mechanic. [1]

The routine is promoted as a way to build trunk endurance while limiting load on the spine, and in posture and looksmaxxing communities it is sometimes included in routines for anterior pelvic tilt and back health. [2]

The sources loaded for this article describe McGill's academic role but do not detail the Big 3 exercises or trials of them, so this article is short. No study found tests the Big 3 for pelvic tilt or appearance.

paras: Stuart McGill's published books on back disorders and fitness include Low Back Disorders: Evidence Based Prevention and Rehabilitation, Ultimate Back Fitness and Performance, Back Mechanic and Gift of Injury. [1] The Big 3 are popularly associated with his spine biomechanics work, but the encyclopedia entry does not describe the exercises.

The bird dog is named in Wikipedia's core stability article as a back-muscle exercise, and the plank as an abdominal exercise. [3] The same article says research support for the core stability model is limited and cites a critical review titled "The myth of core stability". [3]
Wikipedia's pelvic tilt article suggests planks, side planks and dead bugs for anterior pelvic tilt, which overlap in purpose with the Big 3 though not the same movements. [2]
No studies found in the sources loaded for this article. Published work by McGill and colleagues on spinal loading exists but was not reviewed here.
